claim: The brain learns an internal model of the environment through sensory experiences, which is essential for high-level cognitive processes.
source: The brain learns an internal model of the environment through sensory experiences, which is essential for high-level cognitive processes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on internal models in the brain.

claim: Recent studies show that spontaneous activity reflects a learned internal model.
source: Recent studies show that spontaneous activity reflects such a learned internal model.
evidence: This statement references recent studies, implying citation-based support.

claim: Computational studies have proposed that Hebbian plasticity can learn the switching dynamics of replayed activities.
source: Although computational studies have proposed that Hebbian plasticity can learn the switching dynamics of replayed activities, it is still challenging to learn dynamic spontaneous activity that obeys the statistical properties of sensory experience.
evidence: This is supported by references to computational studies.

claim: It is challenging to learn dynamic spontaneous activity that obeys the statistical properties of sensory experience.
source: Although computational studies have proposed that Hebbian plasticity can learn the switching dynamics of replayed activities, it is still challenging to learn dynamic spontaneous activity that obeys the statistical properties of sensory experience.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field based on existing literature.

claim: The proposed synaptic plasticity rule for excitatory synapses seeks to minimize the discrepancy between stimulus-evoked and internally predicted activity.
source: The proposed synaptic plasticity rule for excitatory synapses seeks to minimize the discrepancy between stimulus-evoked and internally predicted activity, while inhibitory plasticity maintains the excitatory-inhibitory balance.
evidence: This describes the model proposed in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity maintains the excitatory-inhibitory balance.
source: The proposed synaptic plasticity rule for excitatory synapses seeks to minimize the discrepancy between stimulus-evoked and internally predicted activity, while inhibitory plasticity maintains the excitatory-inhibitory balance.
evidence: This describes the role of inhibitory plasticity in the proposed model.

claim: The spontaneous reactivation of cell assemblies follows the transition statistics of the model's evoked dynamics.
source: We show that the spontaneous reactivation of cell assemblies follows the transition statistics of the model's evoked dynamics.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated in the manuscript with simulation data.

claim: Simulations of the model can replicate recent experimental results of spontaneous activity in songbirds.
source: We also demonstrate that simulations of our model can replicate recent experimental results of spontaneous activity in songbirds, suggesting that the proposed plasticity rule might underlie the mechanism by which animals learn internal models of the environment.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison with experimental data from songbirds.

claim: The proposed plasticity rule might underlie the mechanism by which animals learn internal models of the environment.
source: We also demonstrate that simulations of our model can replicate recent experimental results of spontaneous activity in songbirds, suggesting that the proposed plasticity rule might underlie the mechanism by which animals learn internal models of the environment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the model's implications.

claim: The brain is thought to use its sensory experience to learn an appropriate internal model of the environment, which can improve perception and behavioral performance.
source: The brain is thought to use its sensory experience to learn an appropriate internal model of the environment, which can improve perception and behavioral performance. (Merfeld et al., 1999; Lewald and Ehrenstein, 1998; Bell et al., 1997; Yasui and Young, 1975; Wolpert et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Learning internal models is thought to be fundamental to higher-order cognitive processes such as perception, decision making, and prediction of sensory stimuli.
source: Such learning is thought to be fundamental to higher-order cognitive processes such as perception, decision making, and prediction of sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of internal models based on established knowledge.

claim: In the visual cortex of awake ferrets, spontaneous activity shows spatial similarity to activity elicited by natural scenes.
source: For example, in the visual cortex of awake ferrets, spontaneous activity shows spatial similarity to activity elicited by natural scenes (Berkes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berkes et al., 2011.

claim: Hippocampus generates sequential replay of place fields during rest and sleep.
source: Furthermore, hippocampus generates sequential replay of place fields during rest and sleep (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Lee and Wilson, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Hippocampal replay occurs in a highly stereotyped temporal order, with the same sequence of replayed activities often observed across multiple events.
source: Such hippocampal replay occurs in a highly stereotyped temporal order, with the same sequence of replayed activities often observed across multiple events (Davidson et al., 2009; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Gupta et al., 2010; Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Several computational studies have proposed variants of Hebbian plasticity rules for learning deterministic or even stochastic switching dynamics of replayed activities.
source: Several computational studies have proposed variants of Hebbian plasticity rules for learning deterministic or even stochastic switching dynamics of replayed activities (Levy et al., 2001; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Triplett et al., 2018; Ocker and Doiron, 2019; Asabuki and Fukai, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior computational work.

claim: It has been challenging to extend these results to generate dynamic spontaneous activity obeying appropriate transition probabilities learned through sensory experience.
source: However, it has been challenging to extend these results to generate dynamic spontaneous activity obeying appropriate transition probabilities learned through sensory experience.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior work.

claim: Finding a plasticity rule which is capable of learning structured transitions in spontaneous activity could be instrumental for understanding the mechanism underlying cognitive processes in the brain.
source: Finding a plasticity rule which is capable of learning structured transitions in spontaneous activity could be instrumental for understanding the mechanism underlying cognitive processes in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of such a plasticity rule.

claim: The proposed plasticity rule is local and biologically plausible.
source: In this paper, we propose a local biologically plausible plasticity rule for learning the statistical transitions between assemblies in spontaneous activity.
evidence: This describes a key property of the proposed model.

claim: The recurrent spiking neural network model consists of distinct excitatory and inhibitory populations.
source: We use a recurrent spiking neural network model consisting of distinct excitatory and inhibitory populations.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the model.

claim: The trained model exhibits spontaneous stochastic transitions of cell assemblies, even after structured external inputs are removed.
source: Our results show that the trained model exhibits spontaneous stochastic transitions of cell assemblies, even after structured external inputs are removed.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The transition statistics of spontaneous activity show a striking similarity to those of the evoked dynamics.
source: We show that the transition statistics of spontaneous activity show a striking similarity to those of the evoked dynamics.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: Recent experimental results in songbirds show that the uncertainty of upcoming states in a bird song modulates the degree of neural predictability.
source: To further validate our model, we compare the model behavior with recent experimental results in songbirds (Bouchard and Brainard, 2016), which show that the uncertainty of upcoming states in a bird song modulates the degree of neural predictability.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bouchard and Brainard, 2016.

claim: The model replicates the experimental result that uncertainty modulates neural predictability in songbirds.
source: Our model replicates this experimental result, suggesting that the connectivity structure learned via the proposed plasticity mechanism could plausibly underlie the songbird's learned internal model.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison with experimental data.

claim: The connectivity structure learned via the proposed plasticity mechanism could plausibly underlie the songbird's learned internal model.
source: Our model replicates this experimental result, suggesting that the connectivity structure learned via the proposed plasticity mechanism could plausibly underlie the songbird's learned internal model.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the model's implications.

claim: Most studies have investigated plasticity mechanisms for learning random switching or deterministic transitions between cell assemblies.
source: While most studies have investigated plasticity mechanisms for learning random switching (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Triplett et al., 2018; Ocker and Doiron, 2019; Asabuki and Fukai, 2024) or deterministic transitions (Chadwick et al., 2015) between cell assemblies, our objective is to create a network model that spontaneously replays stochastic sequences of assemblies following synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The objective is to create a network model that spontaneously replays stochastic sequences of assemblies following synaptic plasticity.
source: While most studies have investigated plasticity mechanisms for learning random switching (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Triplett et al., 2018; Ocker and Doiron, 2019; Asabuki and Fukai, 2024) or deterministic transitions (Chadwick et al., 2015) between cell assemblies, our objective is to create a network model that spontaneously replays stochastic sequences of assemblies following synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This describes the goal of the study.

claim: A non-overlapping subset of excitatory network neurons receive their preferred stimulus.
source: We assume that a non-overlapping subset of excitatory network neurons receive its preferred stimulus (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the stimulus configuration in the model, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: After learning, the network should replay stochastic sequences of assemblies with transitions that are statistically consistent with evoked dynamics, without relying on external stimuli.
source: After learning, the network should replay stochastic sequences of assemblies with transitions that are statistically consistent with evoked dynamics, without relying on external stimuli (Figure 1a, bottom).
evidence: This describes the expected outcome of the model, illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The network model consists of excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) model neurons.
source: Our network model consists of excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) model neurons (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the architecture of the model, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Only excitatory neurons are driven by external stochastic sequences.
source: Only excitatory neurons are driven by external stochastic sequences.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model.

claim: Initially, neurons in the network have random recurrent connections.
source: Initially, neurons in the network have random recurrent connections.
evidence: This describes the initial state of the model.

claim: Only connections onto excitatory neurons were plastic.
source: We assumed that only connections onto excitatory neurons were plastic (Figure 1b), while all others (i.e. connections onto inhibitory neurons) were fixed.
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the model, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: All synaptic weights in the excitatory recurrent connectivity were modified to reduce the error between internally generated and stimulus-evoked activities.
source: In the excitatory recurrent connectivity, all synaptic weights were modified to reduce the error between internally generated and stimulus-evoked activities (Figure 1c, blue square).
evidence: This describes the excitatory plasticity rule, illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: The plasticity rule is mathematically similar to that proposed in Pfister et al., 2006; Urbanczik and Senn, 2014.
source: This plasticity rule is mathematically similar to that proposed in Pfister et al., 2006; Urbanczik and Senn, 2014, which minimizes the discrepancy between the somatic and dendritic activities (Asabuki and Fukai, 2020; Asabuki and Fukai, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Excitatory synapses that contribute to predicting neural activity will be strengthened, thereby increasing the similarity between spontaneous and evoked activity.
source: Through this process, excitatory synapses that contribute to predicting neural activity will be strengthened, thereby increasing the similarity between spontaneous and evoked activity.
evidence: This is an inference about how the plasticity rule works.

claim: Inhibitory synapses were modified to predict the recurrent excitatory potential.
source: Instead of predicting the firing rate of neurons, the inhibitory synapses were modified to predict the recurrent excitatory potential (Figure 1c, orange square).
evidence: This describes the inhibitory plasticity rule, illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity is crucial for the network to maintain excitatory-inhibitory balance.
source: This inhibitory plasticity is crucial for the network to maintain excitatory-inhibitory balance (Vogels et al., 2011) and generate spontaneous replay of stochastic assembly sequences, as we will see later.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and will be demonstrated later in the manuscript.

claim: All feedforward connections were fixed and receptive fields were preconfigured.
source: All feedforward connections were fixed and receptive fields were preconfigured.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model.

claim: Parameters of the response function are regulated according to the activity history of individual neurons.
source: Finally, as in the previous study (Asabuki and Fukai, 2024), parameters of the response function are regulated according to the activity history of individual neurons (Methods).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and described in the Methods.

claim: This regulation maintains the appropriate dynamic range of activities irrespective of the strength of external stimuli.
source: This regulation maintains the appropriate dynamic range of activities irrespective of the strength of external stimuli.
evidence: This describes the function of the regulation mechanism.

claim: External inputs were generated by first-order Markovian chains with three 200ms long states, governed by fixed transition probabilities.
source: These inputs were generated by first-order Markovian chains with three 200ms long states, governed by fixed transition probabilities (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes the stimulus protocol, shown in Figure 2a.

claim: During training, excitatory synapses were modified much quicker than inhibitory synapses.
source: During training, excitatory synapses were modified much quicker than inhibitory synapses (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2b.

claim: The difference in plasticity timescales follows from the nature of the learning rules: the wiring of excitatory synapses is reorganized by external stimuli, while inhibitory synapses only change to rebalance excitation.
source: This difference in plasticity timescales follows from the nature of our learning rules: the wiring of excitatory synapses is reorganized by external stimuli, while inhibitory synapses only change to rebalance excitation.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the observed timescale difference.

claim: Excitatory plasticity in the model occurs before inhibitory plasticity, consistent with experimental results.
source: As such, excitatory plasticity in our model occurs before inhibitory plasticity, consistent with the experimental results (D'amour and Froemke, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Even when the learning rate of inhibitory plasticity was twice that of excitatory plasticity, inhibitory plasticity still occurred on a slower timescale than excitatory plasticity.
source: Indeed, even when the learning rate of inhibitory plasticity was twice that of excitatory plasticity, inhibitory plasticity still occurred on a slower timescale than excitatory plasticity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Before learning, all excitatory neurons showed synchronous and spatially unstructured spontaneous activity.
source: Before learning, due to uniform initial connectivity, all excitatory neurons showed synchronous and spatially unstructured spontaneous activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: After learning, three cell assemblies emerged in the network, each of which encoded one external stimulus.
source: However, after learning, three cell assemblies emerged in the network, each of which encoded one external stimulus.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: Sequences of cell assemblies were replayed stochastically in spontaneous activity.
source: Sequences of these cell assemblies were replayed stochastically in spontaneous activity (Figure 2c), and durations of given assembly reactivations were biased toward shorter durations but distributed broadly (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 2c and 2d.

claim: Durations of given assembly reactivations were biased toward shorter durations but distributed broadly.
source: Sequences of these cell assemblies were replayed stochastically in spontaneous activity (Figure 2c), and durations of given assembly reactivations were biased toward shorter durations but distributed broadly (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2d.

claim: Immediately after the reactivation of assembly 3 ceased, currents onto both subsequent assemblies (1 and 2) increased gradually, without showing a significant difference.
source: Immediately after the reactivation of assembly 3 ceased, currents onto both subsequent assemblies increased gradually, without showing a significant difference (Figure 2e, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2e, left.

claim: State 1 and state 2 are structurally symmetrical in the setting shown in Figure 2a.
source: This is due to the fact that state 1 and state 2 are structurally symmetrical in our setting (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the task structure shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Assembly 3 was driven much more strongly than assembly 2 after reactivation of assembly 1.
source: Consistent with this bias between transition probabilities, we found that assembly 3 was driven much strongly than assembly 2 (Figure 2e, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2e, right.

claim: The temporal statistics of the trained external sequence influence the strength of synaptic currents that drive each assembly.
source: These results suggest that the temporal statistics of the trained external sequence influence the strength of synaptic currents that drive each assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed relationship between transition probabilities and synaptic currents.

claim: Comparison between transition probabilities of stimulus patterns and that of the reactivated assemblies revealed a clear alignment of temporal statistics.
source: Comparison between transition probabilities of stimulus patterns and that of the reactivated assemblies revealed a clear alignment of temporal statistics (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2f.

claim: Even when the network was trained with input states of half the duration, the distributions of the durations of assembly reactivations remain almost identical to those in the original case.
source: Interestingly, even when the network was trained with input states of half the duration, the distributions of the durations of assembly reactivations remain almost identical to those in the original case (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The transition probabilities in the replay were still consistent with the true transition probabilities when trained with input states of half the duration.
source: Furthermore, the transition probabilities in the replay were still consistent with the true transition probabilities (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3b.

claim: The model can learn appropriate transition statistics as long as the size ratio of the assemblies is not drastically varied.
source: These results suggest that the model can learn appropriate transition statistics as long as the size ratio of the assemblies is not drastically varied.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulations with different assembly size ratios.

claim: The duration of assembly became longer in the slow learning case than in the fast case.
source: Interestingly, however, we found that the duration of assembly became longer in the slow learning case than in the fast case (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a, c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 5a, c.

claim: Weaker background input causes spontaneous activity with a lower replay rate, which in turn leads to a high variance of the encoded transition.
source: Finally, we found that the weaker background input causes spontaneous activity with a lower replay rate, which in turn leads to a high variance of the encoded transition (Figure 2—figure supplement 6a, b), while stronger inputs make the assembly replay transitions more uniform (Figure 2—figure supplement 6c, d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 6a, b.

claim: Stronger background inputs make the assembly replay transitions more uniform.
source: Finally, we found that the weaker background input causes spontaneous activity with a lower replay rate, which in turn leads to a high variance of the encoded transition (Figure 2—figure supplement 6a, b), while stronger inputs make the assembly replay transitions more uniform (Figure 2—figure supplement 6c, d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 6c, d.

claim: Even with the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory neurons set to 80% and 20%, the network still showed structured spontaneous activity.
source: Even in such a scenario, the network still showed structured spontaneous activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 7a, center), with transition statistics of replayed events matching the true transition probabilities (Figure 2—figure supplement 7a, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 7a.

claim: The network could replay the appropriate transition only under some conditions when plasticity was applied to all synapses.
source: We found the network could replay the appropriate transition only under some conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 7b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 7b.

claim: When the activity of each neuron is triggered by multiple stimuli and has mixed selectivity, the reactivation reproduced the appropriate stochastic transitions.
source: Interestingly, when the activity of each neuron is triggered by multiple stimuli and has mixed selectivity, the reactivation reproduced the appropriate stochastic transitions (Figure 2—figure supplement 7d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 7d.

claim: The plasticity rules in the model learn the transition statistics of evoked patterns while maintaining excitation-inhibition balance.
source: In summary, the plasticity rules in our model learn the transition statistics of evoked patterns while maintaining excitation-inhibition balance.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's function based on the results.

claim: The prediction-based plasticity rule allows the model to learn and spontaneously replay the transition statistics of evoked patterns.
source: Our results show that the prediction-based plasticity rule allows the model to learn and spontaneously replays the transition statistics of evoked patterns.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's function based on the results.

claim: Over the course of training, the average weights of connections in each of the three cell assemblies increased gradually and converged to a strong value.
source: Over the course of training, the average weights of connections in each of the three cell assemblies increased gradually and converged to a strong value (Figure 3a, middle and b, top), indicating the formation of assemblies.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3a, middle and Figure 3b, top.

claim: The average weights between each pair of assemblies decreased and settled at different stationary values.
source: On the other hand, we found that the average weights between each pair of assemblies decreased and settled at different stationary values (Figure 3a, right and b, bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3a, right and Figure 3b, bottom.

claim: The transition probabilities between states should be encoded exclusively via between-assembly connections.
source: After training, we reasoned that the transition probabilities between states should be encoded exclusively via between-assembly connections, as none of the states in the Markovian chain have self-transitions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the task structure.

claim: The average between-assembly connection matrix aligned well to the ground truth probabilities.
source: To test this prediction, we first compared the average between-assembly connection matrix (Figure 3a, right) and the ground truth transition aligned well to the ground truth probabilities (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3a, right and Figure 3d.

claim: The network learns the temporal statistics of sequences by modifying the structure of inter-assembly excitatory connections.
source: These results indicate that the network learns the temporal statistics of sequences by modifying the structure of inter-assembly excitatory connections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed relationship between excitatory weights and transition probabilities.

claim: A model without inhibitory plasticity exhibited spontaneous activity with blurred assembly structures compared to the original model.
source: We found that such a model exhibited spontaneous activity with blurred assembly structures compared to the original model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The transition probabilities between replayed assemblies in the model without inhibitory plasticity did not show clear alignment with true transition.
source: Furthermore, the transition probabilities between replayed assemblies in this case did not show clear alignment with true transition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), though the excitatory weights reached values which did encode transitions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Maintenance of EI balance through inhibitory plasticity is necessary for generating structured spontaneous activity, even if excitatory connections learn transition probabilities.
source: These results suggest that maintenance of EI balance through inhibitory plasticity is necessary for generating structured spontaneous activity, even if excitatory connections learn transition probabilities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of models with and without inhibitory plasticity.

claim: Between-assembly connections converged to certain values to encode task1-matrix during the first half of learning phase.
source: During the first half of learning phase, between-assembly connections converged to certain values to encode task1-matrix (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, bottom, 0–500 s).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, bottom.

claim: Stable connectivity reorganized quickly once the imposed task was switched to task2-matrix.
source: However, such stable connectivity reorganized quickly once the imposed task was switched to task2-matrix (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, bottom, 500–1000 s).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, bottom.

claim: Within-assembly connections did not show reorganization during task switching.
source: Note that in contrast to between-assemblies connections, within-assembly connections did not show such reorganization (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, top).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, top.

claim: The model adapted to the second task even if distinct assembly structures were already formed during the first task.
source: These results indicate that our model adapted to the second task even if distinct assembly structures were already formed during the first task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the task switching results.

claim: Once the task was switched, errors showed an abrupt increase followed by a gradual decrease as the network learned the second task.
source: However, once the task was switched, errors showed an abrupt increase followed by a gradual decrease as the network learned the second task (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c 500-1000 s; Figure 3—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c and 2d.

claim: The peak of inhibitory error occurred delayed after that of excitatory one in each task.
source: Consistent with the previous result (Figure 2b), the peak of inhibitory error occurred delayed after that of excitatory one in each task (D'amour and Froemke, 2015; Vogels et al., 2011; Figure 3—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2d and supported by citations.

claim: The model is capable of task switching, via the reorganization of its weight structures through continuing plasticity.
source: In summary, our model is also capable of task switching, via the reorganization of its weight structures through continuing plasticity.
evidence: This is a summary of the task switching results.

claim: Despite the complex structure of the task shown in Figure 4a, the learned network showed spontaneous reactivations of all assemblies evoked during learning.
source: Despite its complex structure, the learned network showed spontaneous reactivations of all assemblies evoked during learning (Figure 4b), and the transition dynamics between these assemblies were governed by learned transition probabilities (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4b and 4c.

claim: The transition dynamics between assemblies were governed by learned transition probabilities.
source: Despite its complex structure, the learned network showed spontaneous reactivations of all assemblies evoked during learning (Figure 4b), and the transition dynamics between these assemblies were governed by learned transition probabilities (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4c.

claim: The learned weight structures were consistent with the transition probabilities between states.
source: Indeed, the learned weight structures were consistent with the transition probabilities between states as we have seen in simpler task (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recent experimental studies found that human subjects tend to associate a given visual stimulus with other stimuli within the same 'community'.
source: Recent experimental studies which examined temporal community structure (i.e. highly structured graph structure consisting of clusters of densely interconnected nodes; Figure 4d) found that human subjects tend to associate a given visual stimulus with other stimuli within the same 'community' (Schapiro et al., 2013; Pudhiyidath et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The learned model showed stochastic assembly transition during spontaneous activity when trained with temporal community structure.
source: The learned model showed stochastic assembly transition during spontaneous activity (Figure 4e) relying on the appropriate weight structure (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4e and 4f.

claim: Transitions between connected states in the diagram occurred much more frequently than transitions between disconnected states.
source: Although transitions occurred between all pairs of assemblies, transitions between connected states in the diagram occurred much frequently than transitions between disconnected states (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4g.

claim: Plasticity formed strong excitatory connections between assemblies with nonzero transition probabilities.
source: This is because plasticity formed strong excitatory connections between assemblies with nonzero transition probabilities, as shown in Figure 4f.
evidence: This is an inference based on the weight structure shown in Figure 4f.

claim: In human participants, low-dimensional representations of evoked activities in different cortical regions have been reported to show clusters consistent with the structure of communities.
source: In human participants, low-dimensional representations of evoked activities in different cortical regions have been reported to show clusters consistent with the structure of communities (Schapiro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The low-dimensional representations of stimulus patterns were grouped together into clusters or communities of mutually predictive stimuli, consistent with the experimental results.
source: Such analysis revealed that the representations of stimulus patterns were grouped together into clusters or communities of mutually predictive stimuli, consistent with the experimental results (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4h and compared to experimental results.

claim: The clustered representations still exist even if the input sequences were scrambled after learning.
source: We found that the clustered representations still exist even if the input sequences were scrambled after learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), indicating that this result does not rely on the stimulus protocol, but instead on the learned weights.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Within-community reactivations should occur quicker than between-community assemblies, due to strong within-community coupling.
source: According to the above results, we expect that within-community reactivations should occur quicker than between-community assemblies, due to strong within-community coupling.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the learned weight structure.

claim: The transition to within-community states showed much shorter durations than to between-community case.
source: As expected, the transition to within-community states showed much shorter durations than to between-community case (Figure 4j), indicating that between-community transition occurred with much slower time scale compared to within-community case.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4j.

claim: Between-community transition occurred with much slower time scale compared to within-community case.
source: As expected, the transition to within-community states showed much shorter durations than to between-community case (Figure 4j), indicating that between-community transition occurred with much slower time scale compared to within-community case.
evidence: This is an inference based on the duration measurements shown in Figure 4j.

claim: The network can learn complex temporal structures in spontaneous activity and reproduce the neural representation of the temporal community structure observed in the experiment.
source: Together, these results indicate that our network can learn complex temporal structures in spontaneous activity and reproduce the neural representation of the temporal community structure observed in the experiment.
evidence: This is a summary of the results on temporal community structure.

claim: Bengalese finch learns songs composed of multiple stereotyped short sequences, or syllables.
source: Bf learns songs composed of multiple stereotyped short sequences, or syllables.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Bengalese finch behavior.

claim: The transitions between syllables in Bengalese finch songs can be described via Markovian process with varying levels of certainty.
source: The transitions between these syllables can be described via Markovian process with varying levels of certainty.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Bengalese finch song structure.

claim: Recent experimental study reported that uncertainty of upcoming syllables in a Bengalese finch song modulates the degree of predictability of subsequent neural activation (poststimulus activity; PSA) in HVC.
source: Indeed, recent experimental study reported that uncertainty of upcoming syllables in a Bf song modulates the degree of predictability of subsequent neural activation (poststimulus activity; PSA) in HVC (Bouchard and Brainard, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Next-state correlations were significantly greater than other-state correlations in the highly certain case.
source: Consistent with experimental results, next-state correlations were significantly greater than other-state correlations in the highly certain case (Figure 5b, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5b, left and compared to experimental results.

claim: The correlation difference was less significant in less-certain case.
source: This correlation difference was less significant in less-certain case (Figure 5b, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5b, right.

claim: Transition uncertainty modulated the degree to which PSA is predictive of upcoming states.
source: These results indicate that transition uncertainty modulated the degree to which PSA is predictive of upcoming states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis.

claim: Correlation differences increased as entropy decreased.
source: As expected, correlation differences increased as entropy decreased (Figure 5c), indicating that the predictive strength of network PSA was larger for low-entropy transitions (i.e. highly certain transitions) than for high-entropy transitions (i.e. less-certain transitions).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5c.

claim: The predictive strength of network PSA was larger for low-entropy transitions than for high-entropy transitions.
source: As expected, correlation differences increased as entropy decreased (Figure 5c), indicating that the predictive strength of network PSA was larger for low-entropy transitions (i.e. highly certain transitions) than for high-entropy transitions (i.e. less-certain transitions).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between entropy and correlation differences shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Trial-averaged activities (i.e. PSAs) marginalized all possible transitions in the transition diagram.
source: Although each trial of assembly perturbation lead to subsequent reactivation of one of the assemblies, trial-averaged activities (i.e. PSAs) marginalized all possible transitions in the transition diagram (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying PSA, illustrated in Figure 5a.

claim: Similarities between PSA and stimulus-evoked activities increase if conditional entropy is low (i.e. certain transition), and vice versa.
source: Due to this averaging process, similarities between PSA and stimulus-evoked activities increase if conditional entropy is low (i.e. certain transition), and vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the relationship between entropy and predictability.

claim: The model learns transition statistics of stimulus patterns, with transition uncertainty influencing predictive strength in the network activity.
